> Shultz AJ, Sackton TB (2019). Immune genes are hotspots of shared positive selection across
> birds and mammals. *eLife* 8:e41815. <https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.41815>.
> Open access under CC BY 4.0.
> Read on [PubMed Central](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6338464/).

| Field | |
|---|---|
| **Year** | 2019 |
| **Models** | **39 bird species**, compared against **24 mammal genomes** from Enard et al. 2016 |
| **Brain region** | **None.** A genome-wide scan. The transcriptomes come from pathogen challenge studies in various tissues |
| **Measures** | **DNA** for selection, coding sequence between species. **RNA** for the pathogen challenge data, 26 reanalysed studies in birds and mammals |
| **Method** | Hierarchical orthologous groups across birds. **11,231 genes** run with the gene tree as input, **8,669** with the species tree as input (one sequence per species only) |
| **Cross-species stats** | **PAML** site models (M1a vs M2a, M7 vs M8, M8 vs M8a) and **HyPhy BUSTED**, FDR-corrected p < 0.05. KEGG pathway enrichment. Bird and mammal overlap with Fisher's exact tests and logistic regression |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

## My reading

This paper is about the immune genes. The title is Immune Genes are Hotspots of Shared Positive
Selection Across Birds and Mammals, by Allison J. Shultz and Timothy Sackton at Harvard
University.

What they did is they assumed that there is a **common selective pressure across different
taxa**, and they used alignments of **orthologous protein coding genes from 39 species of
birds** to estimate positive selection across **11,000 genes** conserved across birds. They also
used **pathogen challenge transcriptome data**. They noticed that genes upregulated in, I do not
know what exactly, response to pathogens are also enriched for positively selected genes.
Proteins that interact with viruses experience about **two times as many amino acid changes**
compared to proteins that do not.

Birds are used since they share **convergent features with mammals**, which will be important
later on, because they can actually **cross-reference the enrichment pathways** of positively
selected genes across species.

The methods include comparative genomics in birds, in which they did a **genome-wide scan of
positive selection without any a priori assumptions of gene function**. This is a strong
starting point, because it makes it very clear later on whether their assumption about
positively selected genes and the immune system is correct or not.

They found **four categories where positive selection is high**: the **immune system**, the
**recombination and replication** genes, **lipid metabolism** genes, and **phototransduction**
genes. Their key hypothesis is that **adaptation against pathogens consistently involves the
same genes across evolutionary timescales**, which again allows for the cross-reference of
enrichment of pathways.

They found out that there are **strong signatures of positive selection throughout the avian
genome**. They used **PAML and HyPhy**. They used a **gene tree** as an input tree, and then for
**8,669 genes** they used a **species tree** as an input tree. They used the **dN/dS** parameter,
I believe, and they also used **BUSTED**, which, yeah, maybe not too important for me.

So the immune system, recombination, lipid metabolism and phototransduction pathways are
**enriched for positive selection in birds**. Genes under positive selection have significantly
larger overall **differential expression effect values** compared to those only under positive
selection in birds or those not under positive selection.

**Pathogens drive shared signatures of selection across birds and mammals.** There is a **strong
overlap** in genes with positive selection, and **viruses produce the strongest signature** of
pathogen mediated selection.

## What I take from it

The scan without any a priori assumptions of gene function is a strong starting point, because
it makes it very clear whether their assumption about positively selected genes and the immune
system is correct or not. And using birds allows them to cross-reference the enrichment
pathways of positively selected genes across species.

## Checks against the paper

- **Upregulated in response to what?** Pathogen challenge. They reanalysed 12 bird studies
  covering seven pathogens: four viruses, two bacteria and one protist. Genes upregulated after
  infection were more likely to be under positive selection than genes not differentially
  expressed.
- **Two times as many amino acid changes for virus interacting proteins?** That is a result from
  mammals that they cite, Enard et al. 2016, not a finding of this paper.
- **Genome-wide GWAS?** A genome-wide scan, not a GWAS. A GWAS links variants to a trait within
  one species; this scans every gene for selection across species.
- **11,000 genes, and 8,669 on the species tree?** Yes. 11,231 genes with the gene tree, 8,669
  with the species tree. The species tree set only kept alignments with one sequence per
  species; the gene tree set allowed up to three paralogs.
- **The dN/dS parameter, I believe?** Yes. All the PAML site models and BUSTED test whether some
  sites have dN/dS above 1. 14% of genes passed every test.
- **Four categories?** Yes. 18 KEGG pathways were significantly enriched, and they fall into
  immune, recombination and replication, lipid metabolism and phototransduction.
- **Larger differential expression effect values?** The comparison has three groups: genes under
  selection in **both birds and mammals**, in birds only, or in neither. The genes under
  selection in both had the largest effect values, mostly in response to viruses.
- **Strong overlap between birds and mammals?** Yes, significant at every cutoff they tried, on
  4,931 genes with results in both. It held after removing the most constrained genes and
  accounting for alignment length.

## Open questions from this read

- BUSTED, again marked as not too important for me. Second paper in a row that relies on it.

## How it relates to this project

1. **It uses the same measure.** dN/dS on aligned coding sequence, across a whole genome, is the
   conservation measure this project uses on its BBB genes.

2. **It shows the one sequence per species choice.** The species tree analysis kept only
   alignments with one sequence per species, the same restriction as the one-to-one orthologue
   decision in this project.

3. **It pairs with Nandakumar 2025.** Both papers find immune genes enriched for positive
   selection, one across birds and mammals and one within rodents, and both lean on BUSTED.

## Reference detail from the paper

- **Proportions under positive selection** (gene trees, 11,231 genes): M1a vs M2a 17%, M7 vs M8
  67%, M8 vs M8a 33%, BUSTED 56%, all tests 1,562 genes (14%). Species trees: 1,203 of 8,669
  (14%) in all tests.
- **Overall ω** (M0 model): mean 0.15, median 0.10. Median 0.344 for genes under selection
  against 0.084 for the rest.
- **Alignment length:** longer genes were more often under selection, likely more power to
  detect it.
- **Pathway enrichment:** 351 selected genes and 3,347 background genes mapped to KEGG with
  chicken as reference; 18 pathways enriched at q < 0.1.
- **Bird and mammal transcriptomes:** significant overlap in upregulated genes for influenza A,
  West Nile virus, E. coli and Mycoplasma; none in downregulated genes for viruses or bacteria.
- **Classic host pathogen genes under selection in both clades** and upregulated after
  infection: PKR, PARP9, MX1.
